question: How can I upskill managers across my company without building courses in-house?
text:
Yes. You can build a strong manager-development system without creating your own courses. The trick is to outsource the content and facilitation, while keeping ownership of the manager standards, participant selection, practice, and measurement internally.

A practical model
1. Buy a proven core program

Instead of building 10–20 internal courses, choose an external provider with an existing manager curriculum.

For example:

Center for Creative Leadership offers programs for frontline, mid-level and senior leaders, including live-online and in-person formats. It also offers enterprise-scale content and customized cohorts. 
C
CCL
+1

FranklinCovey offers an enterprise content subscription, instructor-led training, coaching and a train-the-trainer option. 
F
FranklinCovey

For a DACH-focused approach, providers such as Schuppan offer in-house, live-online and coaching formats. 
S
Schuppan Management

You don't necessarily need the same provider for every level.

2. Segment managers by level

I'd avoid one generic "Manager Academy."

A simple architecture is:

Population	Development focus
New managers	1:1s, feedback, delegation, performance conversations, team basics
Experienced managers	Coaching, conflict, influencing, prioritization, developing talent
Senior managers	Strategy, organizational change, cross-functional leadership, succession
High potentials	Broader enterprise perspective, strategic projects, executive exposure

For example, CCL explicitly distinguishes programs for emerging/frontline, mid-level and senior leaders. 
C
CCL

3. Make the vendor provide the "course," not the whole development experience

This is the important bit.

A manager shouldn't simply attend six workshops and receive a certificate. Use a structure like:

External content → cohort session → real work → manager/peer practice → reflection → repeat

For example, a 10-week journey could be:

External provider: managing performance

Apply it to one real employee situation

Peer practice group

Manager's manager observes/checks in

External provider: difficult conversations

Apply to a real conversation

Peer case clinic

External provider: delegation/coaching

Action-learning project

Reflection + development plan

The external provider supplies the expertise and learning assets; your organization supplies the context and application.

4. Establish 5–8 non-negotiable management behaviors internally

This is the piece I'd not outsource.

For example, CCL explicitly distinguishes programs for emerging/frontline, mid-level and senior leaders. 
C
CCL

Every manager at our company is expected to set clear expectations, hold regular 1:1s, give timely feedback, address performance issues early, develop people, and create an inclusive team environment.

Then make the external curriculum reinforce those behaviors.

That prevents the classic problem where employees attend a prestigious leadership course but return to an organization with completely different management expectations.

5. Use different purchasing models

You have several options:

A. Enterprise library

Buy access to a large external library and let managers consume relevant material. FranklinCovey, for example, offers an All Access Pass containing content, assessments, tools and videos. 
F
FranklinCovey

Best when you have hundreds/thousands of managers and need broad coverage.

B. Cohort program

Buy an existing program and run cohorts of 15–30 managers.

Best when you want behavior change rather than content consumption.

CCL, for example, offers open-enrollment programs as well as customized organizational cohorts. 
C
CCL

Have the provider certify a small number of your HR/L&D people to deliver its existing material. FranklinCovey explicitly offers this model. 
F
FranklinCovey

Curriculum for new, experienced and senior managers

Live vs asynchronous delivery

Global/DACH delivery capability

Cohort size

Facilitator quality and consistency

Assessments/360s

Coaching options

Manager-of-participant involvement

Application between sessions

Measurement of behavioral change

Localization/customization

LMS/LXP integration

Pricing at 100 / 500 / 1,000 managers

Train-the-trainer/licensing options

References from organizations of similar scale

Then pilot one cohort of ~20–30 managers before committing to an enterprise rollout.

The key principle is: don't build a manager academy; build a manager-development system and plug external content into it. That gives you the speed and quality of specialist providers without giving up control of what "good management" means in your company.
